q: What is a doubly reinforced beam?
o: A beam with compression steel as well as tension steel
A beam with two layers of tension bars only
A beam reinforced with both stirrups and ties
A beam cast together with its slab
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Compression bars near the top help the concrete carry compression. They are used when the beam depth is limited and a singly reinforced section cannot reach the needed moment, and they also reduce long-term (creep) deflection.

q: What is the base diameter of the standard slump cone?
o: 100 mm (4 in)
200 mm (8 in)
150 mm (6 in)
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: The ASTM C143 slump cone is 300 mm tall, 200 mm across the base and 100 mm across the top. Keep them apart: 300 high, 200 bottom, 100 top.

q: Under ASTM C94, within what time after batching should ready-mixed concrete normally be fully discharged?
o: 30 minutes
3 hours
90 minutes
6 hours
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: ASTM C94 asks for discharge within 1½ hours (or before 300 drum revolutions) after water first meets the cement. After that the mix stiffens. A project specification may allow more time with retarders or less time in hot weather.

q: Why do codes guard against shear failure in beams more strictly than flexural failure?
o: Shear failure always happens at midspan, where it is hard to see
Shear failure only happens in steel beams
Shear failure is slow and ductile, so it is hard to detect
Shear failure is brittle and can happen suddenly, with little warning
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: A beam that fails in shear cracks diagonally and can collapse abruptly, while an under-reinforced beam failing in bending sags and cracks visibly first. That is why the shear strength reduction factor (φ = 0.75) is lower than the one for bending (0.90).

q: In strength design, how is the required (ultimate) strength U found?
o: By multiplying the service loads by load factors in the code load combinations
By adding all the service loads with no factors
By dividing the service loads by a factor of safety
By multiplying only the live load by 2
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: U comes from load combinations such as U = 1.4D or U = 1.2D + 1.6L (NSCP 203.3). Different loads get different factors because some are more uncertain than others. The member is then designed so that φ times its nominal strength is at least U.

q: What is a "rich" concrete mix?
o: A mix with a high water-cement ratio
A mix with a relatively high cement content
A mix with extra coarse aggregate
A mix with no admixtures
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: A rich mix has more cement for its volume, such as Class AA (1 : 1½ : 3), so it is stronger but costlier and shrinks more. A lean mix, such as Class C (1 : 3 : 6), has less cement.

q: What is the development length of a reinforcing bar?
o: The length of the hook bent at the bar's end
The overlap between two spliced bars
The embedment needed for bond to build up the bar's full design stress
The distance between two adjacent bars
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: A bar can only pull as hard as the concrete around it can grip it. The development length ld is how far it must be embedded past the point of maximum stress so bond can develop fy. It grows with bar size and fy and shrinks with higher f'c.

q: Why is an under-reinforced beam section preferred in design?
o: The concrete crushes first, which is quick and clean
It uses the most steel possible
It never cracks under service loads
The tension steel yields before the concrete crushes, so the beam gives warning before it fails
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: In an under-reinforced (tension-controlled) section the steel yields first. The beam deflects and cracks widely, warning the occupants long before collapse. The code encourages this by giving the highest φ (0.90) to tension-controlled sections.

q: In the figure of slump-test results, which one is a shear slump?
o: Shape B
Shape A
Shape C
None of them
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: In a shear slump (B), one side of the concrete slides off along a slanted plane. It points to a harsh mix that lacks cohesion. ASTM C143 treats it as an invalid result, so the test is repeated with a fresh sample.

q: Why are concrete and steel combined in reinforced concrete?
o: Steel is strong in compression and concrete carries the tension
Concrete is strong in compression and steel carries the tension
Both are weak in tension, so they share it
Steel only protects the concrete from fire
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Concrete's tensile strength is only about a tenth of its compressive strength, so it cracks under tension. Steel bars placed in the tension zone take over after cracking. The two work together because they bond well and expand with heat at almost the same rate.

q: What is a singly reinforced beam?
o: A beam with only one bar
A beam with steel only in the compression zone
A beam with longitudinal steel only in the tension zone
A beam with no stirrups
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: A singly reinforced beam relies on the concrete alone for compression and puts its main bars in the tension zone. It is the common case; compression steel is added (doubly reinforced) only when needed.

q: What is the top diameter of the standard slump cone?
o: 200 mm (8 in)
120 mm (5 in)
100 mm (4 in)
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: The top opening of the ASTM C143 cone is 100 mm (4 in); the base is 200 mm and the height 300 mm. 120 mm is a common wrong figure: 4 inches is about 102 mm.

q: Which admixture delays the setting of concrete?
o: Retarder
Accelerator
Air-entraining agent
Superplasticizer
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Retarders slow setting, which helps in hot weather, for long hauls and to avoid cold joints in large pours. Accelerators do the opposite, and air-entraining agents add tiny bubbles for freeze-thaw resistance.

q: In a T-beam under positive moment, which part works as the compression flange?
o: The web below the slab
The effective width of the slab cast with the beam
The stirrups
The bottom tension bars
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: When the slab is cast monolithically with the beam, a strip of slab (the effective flange width) carries the compression at the top. The web below it holds the tension steel. Under negative moment the flange is in tension, so the beam acts as a rectangle.

q: What is the height of the standard slump cone?
o: 200 mm (8 in)
100 mm (4 in)
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: The cone is 300 mm tall. It is filled in three layers of equal volume, each rodded 25 times, then lifted straight up in about 5 seconds, and the drop of the concrete is measured.

q: How is the dosage of a chemical admixture decided?
o: Always 3% of the total concrete volume
Always 1 liter per cubic meter, whatever the product
By the slump alone, with no reference to the product
From the manufacturer's recommendation and trial mixes, usually per mass of cement
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Each admixture has its own effective range, usually given in mL per 100 kg of cement, and the right amount is confirmed with trial batches. There is no single percentage that fits all admixtures.

q: Under NSCP 2015, which members are exempt from the minimum shear reinforcement required in beams?
o: Solid slabs and footings
Deep transfer girders
All beams deeper than 600 mm
Beams carrying heavy concentrated loads
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: NSCP 2015 Sec. 409.6.3.1 (from ACI 318) exempts solid slabs, footings, joist construction and very shallow beams from minimum stirrups where the factored shear exceeds 0.5φVc. Ordinary beams need at least the minimum stirrups there, because shear failure is brittle.

q: What is a balanced section in reinforced concrete flexure?
o: One where the tension and compression steel have equal areas
One where the tension steel reaches yield just as the concrete reaches its crushing strain of 0.003
One where the beam depth equals its width
One with steel only at mid-depth
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: At balance, the steel yields (εy = fy/Es) at the same moment the extreme concrete fibre reaches 0.003. More steel than that gives an over-reinforced, brittle beam; less gives an under-reinforced, ductile one.

q: In the figure of slump-test results, which one is a true slump?
o: Shape B
Shape C
Shape A
All three
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: In a true slump (A) the concrete settles evenly and keeps roughly its cone shape. Only this form gives a valid slump reading, measured from the top of the cone to the top of the settled concrete.

q: What single factor has the strongest effect on the strength and durability of hardened concrete?
o: The size of the mixer
The color of the aggregate
The slump cone used for testing
The water-cement ratio
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Abrams' law: as the water-cement ratio rises, strength falls, because the extra water leaves pores when it evaporates. More pores also let water and chlorides in, so durability suffers too.

q: How does NSCP 2015 keep beams from being over-reinforced?
o: By requiring a net tensile strain in the steel of at least 0.004
By banning compression steel
By requiring the beam depth to equal twice the width
By limiting the concrete strength to 21 MPa
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Flexural members must have εt ≥ 0.004 at nominal strength (NSCP 409.3.3.1). To get the full φ = 0.90 the section must be tension-controlled, with εt ≥ 0.005. Both limits keep the steel yielding before the concrete crushes.

q: A slump test on a normal-weight column mix gives a collapse slump. What should be concluded?
o: The mix is ideal for columns
The mix is too wet for a valid slump reading, so the mix should be checked
The result is a valid slump of 300 mm
The concrete is too stiff and needs more cement
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: A collapse means the concrete spread out entirely, usually because of too much water. The test cannot measure it, and for ordinary concrete it signals a mix problem. Very fluid mixes such as self-consolidating concrete are checked with a slump-flow test instead.

q: Which admixture speeds up setting and early strength gain?
o: Retarder
Air-entraining agent
Accelerator
Water reducer
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Accelerators, such as calcium chloride or non-chloride types, shorten setting time and raise early strength, which is useful for early form removal or cold weather. Calcium chloride is not allowed in prestressed concrete or near embedded aluminum because it corrodes metal.

q: What is a T-beam?
o: A beam with a T-shaped steel section inside
A beam supported at three points
A beam used only for roof trusses
A beam cast together with the slab, so part of the slab acts as its compression flange
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: In monolithic construction the slab and beam act as one. The slab strip over the beam forms the flange of the T and the part below the slab forms the web. An edge beam with a slab on one side only is called an L-beam.

q: In a typical concrete mix, which ingredient takes up the largest share of the volume?
o: Coarse aggregate (gravel)
Fine aggregate (sand)
Water
Cement
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Aggregates fill about 60 to 75% of concrete's volume, and coarse aggregate is the largest single part, commonly around 35 to 40%. Cement is only about 10 to 15%. The exact split comes from the mix design.

q: What is the role of shear reinforcement (stirrups) in a concrete beam?
o: It carries the main bending moment at midspan
It resists diagonal tension from shear and helps confine the concrete and hold the main bars
It prevents the slab from lifting off the beam
It controls shrinkage along the top surface
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Stirrups cross the diagonal cracks that shear causes near the supports and carry the tension across them. They also hold the longitudinal bars in place and add some confinement to the concrete.

q: In strength design, how is the design strength of a member obtained?
o: By dividing the nominal strength by the load factor
By adding a safety margin of 10 kN
By multiplying the nominal strength by a strength reduction factor φ
By using the nominal strength with no reduction
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Design strength = φ × nominal strength (φMn, φVn, φPn) and must be at least the required strength U. φ reflects how reliable and how ductile each mode is: 0.90 for tension-controlled bending, 0.75 for shear, 0.65 for tied columns.

q: What does the slump test measure?
o: The compressive strength of hardened concrete
The air content of fresh concrete
The unit weight of hardened concrete
The consistency (workability) of fresh concrete
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Slump shows how stiff or fluid a fresh mix is and whether batches are consistent. It is not a strength test; strength is checked by crushing cylinders, usually at 28 days.

q: What is concrete made of?
o: Cement, water, fine aggregate and coarse aggregate, with optional admixtures
Cement, lime and sand only
Cement and water only
Sand, gravel and lime only
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Cement and water form a paste that hardens by hydration and binds the sand and gravel. Admixtures may be added to change workability, setting time or durability. Cement, lime and sand without gravel make mortar or plaster, not concrete.

q: What is an over-reinforced beam section?
o: One with more stirrups than the code minimum
One with so much tension steel that the concrete crushes before the steel yields
One with compression steel added
One with steel placed below the required cover
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: With too much steel, the steel is still elastic when the concrete reaches 0.003 strain and crushes. The failure is sudden, with little deflection or cracking to warn anyone, so codes do not allow it.

q: In the figure of slump-test results, which one is a collapse slump?
o: Shape A
Shape B
Shape C
None of them
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: In a collapse slump (C) the concrete loses its shape and spreads out. It usually means the mix is too wet, and it does not give a valid slump value.

q: What is an admixture in concrete?
o: Any aggregate finer than 4.75 mm
The water added after the mixer leaves the plant
The steel reinforcement
An ingredient other than cement, water and aggregate, added to change the concrete's properties
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Admixtures are added just before or during mixing to adjust properties: retarders and accelerators change the setting time, water reducers improve workability, and air-entraining agents add freeze-thaw resistance.

q: A ready-mix truck arrives 2 hours after batching and the concrete has stiffened. What should be done?
o: Reject it or refer it to the engineer, since it is past the normal 90-minute limit
Add water at the site until it flows
Pour it into columns, where stiff concrete is better
Mix in more cement by hand
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (ACI 318-14 basis); ASTM C143 slump test; ASTM C94 ready-mixed concrete
n: Adding water raises the water-cement ratio and cuts strength. ASTM C94 sets a normal limit of 90 minutes from batching, so concrete this late is usually rejected unless the engineer approves otherwise (for example, when a retarder was used).
